newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Soft commodities surge, rest can only look on.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Soft commodities surge, rest can only look on.

text.p: Cocoa and coffee charged ahead on Wednesday, breaking out of a post-Easter rut and leaving other commodities behind.
Cocoa was pushed higher by speculators and broke through technical resistance to race to the highest level since August last year. Benchmark May futures closed up 30 stg at 1,047
But a fall on Wall Street failed to see investors bailing out of stocks move into commmodities markets, with the metals particularly quiet.
Trade on the London Metal Exchange was soggy at best. Copper nudged higher but failed to inspire any radical moves amongst the other base metals.
Zinc fell off a fresh 4-1/2 year high set in the morning while nickel and aluminium made only modest gains. But analysts said the future was brighter.
"Copper is looking for new impetus. It and the others (base metals) are showing an upward bias after testing the lower end of the range," said Martin Squires of broker Rudolf Wolff.
Coffee marched ahead in morning London trade but volumes were thin as investors remained wary after the market's recent volatility.

The U.S. market called the tune and though prices reached the key $2 a lb level in New York, they retreated later and dragged London back a little too. Producer selling also helped cap the upside, traders said.
Benchmark May robusta futures rose to $1,668 a tonne but then slipped back to close at $1,641, up $27.
Prices were not immediately affected by news that stevedores at Brazil's key port of Santos had gone on strike and traders said it was hard to tell if the market might react later.
"I don't think there will be a major impact as coffee shipments are traditionally slow at this time of the year but you can never say there will be no market impact," said one.
Sugar was a late comer to the soft commodities party and fell in morning trade on pre-EU tender hedging before bouncing back in the afternoon.
Precious metals had a quiet day, stuck between conflicting market views on opposite sides of the Atlantic.
"London and Europe are bearish for gold and silver but New York seems to have a much more bullish view," one London dealer said.
Gold was unaffected by the fall on Wall Street and closed $0.90 higher at $351.35.
While silver wobbled and finished slightly lower at the key $5 level, platinum and palladium put in firmer performances and closed higher.
On the Chicago Board of Trade at midday, May wheat futures were 4-1/4 cents easier at 389-1/2 cents.
Meanwhile, IPE brent fell with May futures 19 cents lower at $18.95 by 1715 GMT.
